course.title: Machine Learning — Zero to Professional
course.subtitle: From your first feature to a production model
course.tagline: A 27-module, ten-section ML school: learn the idea, write the Python, debug it, defend it and ship it.
course.description: This course builds machine learning from the ground up. You start with what learning from data actually means, then Python, NumPy, Pandas, the mathematics and statistics, data preparation, regression, classification, trees and ensembles, evaluation, unsupervised learning, NLP, engineering and deployment. Every module ends with a checkpoint and a defense you can practise. It is designed for a complete beginner who wants entry-level ML Engineer and Data Scientist work, not a vocabulary tour.
outcomes: Explain supervised, unsupervised, semi-supervised and reinforcement learning without hand-waving.
Write clean Python, NumPy and Pandas for real tabular data.
Use the mathematics and statistics that models are actually built from.
Run a complete ML workflow: frame, split, train, evaluate, improve and document.
Build regression, classification, tree, ensemble, clustering, anomaly and NLP models.
Choose an evaluation metric that matches the business cost of mistakes.
Prevent data leakage and build reproducible experiments.
Engineer reusable pipelines and deploy a model behind a validated API.
Explain model decisions, limitations, fairness and privacy risks.
Defend a capstone project in an interview-style conversation.

modules.title: Introduction to Machine Learning
modules.goal: Understand what learning from data means, where ML helps, and the vocabulary every later module uses.

topics.title: What is machine learning?
topics.body: Machine learning is a way to write programs that improve at a task by finding patterns in examples instead of being given every rule by hand. The program is the model; the examples are the data; the answer it produces is the prediction. A model is not magic: it is a mathematical rule whose numbers are fitted from data.
topics.code:
correct = 8
total = 10
print(correct / total)

topics.title: A first learning loop
topics.body: A tiny model can already make predictions. Here the model has learned (or been given) slope 2 and intercept 1, and predicts an output for each input. Real training finds those two numbers from data by minimising error; the prediction step looks exactly like this.
topics.code:
samples = [(1, 3), (2, 5), (3, 7)]
slope = 2
intercept = 1
print([slope * x + intercept for x, _ in samples])

topics.title: Types of machine learning
topics.body: Supervised learning learns from labelled examples (features plus the right answer). Unsupervised learning looks for structure without labels, such as clusters. Semi-supervised learning uses a few labels and many unlabelled examples. Reinforcement learning learns a policy by acting and receiving rewards. Classification predicts a category; regression predicts a number.

interview.q: When should you not use machine learning?
interview.answer: Do not use ML when a deterministic rule is cheaper, auditable and complete; when the data is too small, biased or unavailable; when a single wrong prediction is catastrophic and cannot be reviewed; or when the problem has no learnable pattern. Start with the simplest rule or baseline, and add ML only when measured value justifies its cost and risk.

interview.q: What is the difference between a model parameter and a hyperparameter?
interview.answer: A parameter is learned from the training data, such as a regression weight or a neural-network weight. A hyperparameter is chosen before training, such as a learning rate, tree depth or K in KNN; it controls the learning process and is selected with validation data, never fitted by the training loop itself.

coding.title: Accuracy from two counts
coding.statement: A test set has 15 correct predictions out of 20. Print the accuracy as a decimal.
coding.solution:

total = 20
print(correct / total)
coding.hint: Accuracy is correct predictions divided by all predictions.

coding.title: Positive rate from counts
coding.statement: A test set contains 5 positive examples out of 100. Print the positive rate as a decimal.
coding.solution:

total = 100
print(positives / total)
coding.hint: Divide the positives by the full row count.

defense.q: Why is a baseline required before a complex model?
defense.answer: A baseline turns "the model looks good" into a measurable claim. A majority-class or simple-rule baseline is cheap, exposes class imbalance, and gives the complex model a number it must beat on the same split and metric.

checkpoint.q: Which task is supervised learning?
options: Predicting house price from labelled sales
Learning a game by reward alone
checkpoint.answer: Predicting house price from labelled sales
checkpoint.why: The target price is known in the training examples.

checkpoint.q: A model gets 99% accuracy on a fraud dataset with 1% fraud. What should you check?
options: Precision and recall on the fraud class
checkpoint.answer: Precision and recall on the fraud class
checkpoint.why: A majority-class predictor can score 99% while catching no fraud.

checkpoint.q: True or false: a model that memorises its training labels but fails on new rows is overfitting.
checkpoint.why: Memorising training detail while losing generalisation is the definition of overfitting; the gap between training and validation performance exposes it.

logic.q: A dataset has 95 negative and 5 positive rows. A model predicts negative for every row. What accuracy does it report, and what does that number hide?
logic.answer: It reports 95% accuracy because 95 of 100 rows are negative. It catches zero positives, so recall on the positive class is 0; accuracy alone hides the complete failure on the class that usually matters most.

modules.title: Python Programming for Machine Learning
modules.goal: Write the Python you will use daily: collections, functions, files, errors, packages and a reproducible environment.

topics.title: Functions and comprehensions
topics.body: A function packages a calculation so it can be tested and reused. A list comprehension builds a new list from an iterable in one readable expression. Both appear constantly in feature preparation.
topics.code:
def normalise(marks):
    top = max(marks)
    return [round(mark / top, 2) for mark in marks]
print(normalise([40, 60, 80]))

topics.title: Dictionaries count categories
topics.body: A dictionary maps keys to values. Counting category frequencies with `.get(key, 0) + 1` is a small but essential data-cleaning pattern, and it is the idea behind value counts and vocabulary building.

topics.title: Virtual environments and pip
topics.body: A virtual environment isolates the packages for one project. Create it once, activate it, install exact versions with pip, and record them in requirements.txt. Isolation prevents a course experiment from breaking another project, and pinned versions make an experiment reproducible.

interview.q: What is the difference between a list and a tuple?
interview.answer: A list is mutable and normally holds a homogeneous sequence you will change. A tuple is immutable, can be hashed if its contents are hashable, and is useful for fixed records, multiple return values and dictionary keys. Immutability is a correctness tool, not just a speed choice.

interview.q: Why is a mutable default argument dangerous in Python?
interview.answer: The default object is created once when the function is defined, not once per call. A list or dictionary default is therefore shared across calls, so appending in one call changes what the next caller sees. Use `None` as the sentinel and create the container inside the function.

coding.title: Clean a list of marks
coding.statement: Given marks containing a missing value represented by None, return only the valid marks as floats.
coding.solution:
raw = [80, None, 90, 70]
clean = [float(mark) for mark in raw if mark is not None]
print(clean)
coding.hint: Filter first, then convert.

coding.title: Count unique labels
coding.statement: Given labels ["spam", "ham", "spam"], print the number of distinct labels.
coding.solution:
labels = ["spam", "ham", "spam"]
print(len(set(labels)))
coding.hint: A set keeps one copy of each value.

debug.title: Off-by-one in the mean
debug.broken:
marks = [40, 60, 80]
print(sum(marks) / len(marks) - 1)
debug.error: The result is 59.0 instead of the mean 60.0. The stray `- 1` changes the statistic; remove it rather than adjusting the data.
debug.fix:
marks = [40, 60, 80]
print(sum(marks) / len(marks))

defense.q: Why pin package versions in an ML project?
defense.answer: A model result is only meaningful if the code and data that produced it can be rerun. Pinning prevents a silent library upgrade from changing defaults, metrics or serialization. Record Python, package and dataset versions together; a lockfile is part of the experiment, not paperwork.
steps: Store the lockfile with the experiment.

checkpoint.answer: Python creates the default list or dictionary once when the function is defined, so every call shares the same object. Mutating it in one call changes the value seen by later calls. Use `None` as the default and create a fresh container inside the function.

logic.q: What does `[x * 2 for x in range(3) if x % 2]` evaluate to?
logic.answer: It evaluates to `[2]`: range(3) gives 0, 1 and 2; the filter keeps only the odd value 1, and the expression doubles it.

modules.title: NumPy for Machine Learning
modules.goal: Use ndarrays, vectorised arithmetic, broadcasting, aggregation and linear algebra as the numerical language of ML.

topics.title: Arrays and vectorisation
topics.body: A NumPy array stores numbers in one compact block and applies operations to all elements without a Python loop. Vectorisation is both shorter and faster; it is how feature matrices and model maths are expressed.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([1, 2, 3])
print(a * 2)

interview.q: What is the difference between a NumPy view and a copy?
interview.answer: A view shares the original data buffer; changing it can change the base array. A copy owns new memory. Slicing usually returns a view, while boolean indexing and `.copy()` return a copy. Use `.copy()` when you need independent data, and know which one your preprocessing step produced.

interview.q: What does NumPy broadcasting do when arrays of shape (3, 1) and (1, 4) meet?

modules.title: Pandas for Machine Learning
modules.goal: Load, inspect, filter, group, join and clean tabular data without losing track of rows or types.

topics.title: Series, DataFrames and groupby
topics.body: A Series is one labelled column; a DataFrame is a table of aligned Series. `groupby` splits rows by a key, applies an aggregation and combines the result, which is the fastest way to turn raw transactions into features.
topics.code:
import pandas as pd
df = pd.DataFrame({"city": ["Pune", "Delhi", "Pune"], "marks": [80, 90, 70]})
print(df.groupby("city")["marks"].mean()["Pune"])

topics.title: Finding missing values
topics.body: Missing data is a fact to measure, not an error to hide. `isna().sum()` reports how many values are absent per column; that count decides whether to drop, impute or investigate the collection process.
topics.code:
import pandas as pd
s = pd.Series([10, None, 30])
print(int(s.isna().sum()))

topics.title: Merging, selection and safe assignment
topics.body: Use `merge` for key-based joins, `loc` for label-based selection and `iloc` for position-based selection. Prefer one explicit assignment such as `df.loc[mask, "col"] = value` over chained indexing, which can silently operate on a copy. Always check row counts before and after a join.

interview.q: What is the difference between `.loc` and `.iloc`?
interview.answer: `.loc` selects by index/column labels and supports boolean masks. `.iloc` selects by integer position, like normal Python indexing. Mixing them causes confusing errors, especially with a non-default index; choose based on whether you mean a name or a position.

interview.q: What does Pandas `groupby` actually do internally?
interview.answer: It splits the rows by key, applies the requested aggregation or transformation to each group, and combines the results into a new Series or DataFrame. Group keys that are missing are excluded by default, which is why a null category can silently disappear from a report.

topics.title: Vectors, dot products and predictions
topics.body: A feature row and a weight vector are both vectors. Their dot product multiplies matching entries and adds them, producing one prediction. This one operation underlies linear regression, logistic regression and every neural-network layer.

topics.title: A gradient descent step
topics.body: A gradient points in the direction of steepest increase. To reduce a loss, move the parameter in the opposite direction, scaled by a learning rate. One step is `w_new = w - learning_rate * gradient`.

topics.title: Derivatives, chain rule and loss
topics.body: A derivative measures how a tiny change in an input changes an output. The chain rule composes those rates through nested operations, which is exactly what backpropagation does. A loss function turns "how wrong" into a number that optimisation can reduce; mean squared error and log loss are two common choices.

interview.q: Why do we subtract the gradient instead of adding it?
interview.answer: The gradient points toward increasing loss. Training wants lower loss, so we step in the negative-gradient direction. The learning rate controls the step size; too large can overshoot, too small is slow.

interview.q: What is the difference between a derivative and a gradient?
interview.answer: A derivative measures how a scalar output changes with one scalar input. A gradient collects the partial derivatives with respect to every parameter into a vector; it points in the direction of steepest increase, which is why training moves in the opposite direction.

modules.title: Probability and Statistics
modules.goal: Describe uncertainty, compare groups and interpret evidence instead of trusting a single average.

topics.title: Mean and standard deviation
topics.body: The mean is the balance point of a distribution; standard deviation describes typical distance from it. Together they summarise centre and spread, and they are the basis of standardisation and z-scores.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
xs = np.array([2, 4, 6])
print(float(np.mean(xs)), round(float(np.std(xs)), 2))

topics.title: Bayes theorem in one calculation
topics.body: Bayes updates a prior belief with evidence. The posterior is prior × likelihood ÷ evidence. It is the foundation of Naive Bayes and of reasoning about false positives in medical or fraud screening.
topics.code:
prior = 0.1
likelihood = 0.8
evidence = 0.2
print(round(prior * likelihood / evidence, 2))

topics.title: Sampling, intervals and hypothesis tests
topics.body: A sample statistic varies from sample to sample. A confidence interval expresses that uncertainty, while a hypothesis test asks whether an observed difference is plausible under a null model. A p-value is not the probability that the null is true, and statistical significance is not business importance.

interview.q: What does a p-value actually mean?
interview.answer: It is the probability of observing data at least as extreme as ours, assuming the null hypothesis is true. It is not the probability that the null is true, nor the probability of replication. Report an effect size and interval alongside it.

interview.q: What is the difference between standard deviation and standard error?
interview.answer: Standard deviation describes the spread of individual observations around the mean. Standard error describes the uncertainty of an estimated statistic, commonly the mean, and shrinks roughly as 1/√n as the sample grows.

coding.title: A Bayes update
coding.statement: A prior of 0.2 and likelihood of 0.5 meet evidence 0.25. Print the posterior rounded to two decimals.
coding.solution:
prior = 0.2
likelihood = 0.5
evidence = 0.25
print(round(prior * likelihood / evidence, 2))
coding.hint: Multiply prior by likelihood, then divide by evidence.

coding.title: Standard error of the mean
coding.statement: For [2, 4, 6], print the sample standard error of the mean, rounded to three decimals.
coding.starter:
import math
import statistics
xs = [2, 4, 6]
# print the standard error
coding.solution:
import math
import statistics
xs = [2, 4, 6]
print(round(statistics.stdev(xs) / math.sqrt(len(xs)), 3))
coding.hint: Sample standard deviation divided by the square root of n.

topics.title: Univariate, bivariate and multivariate views
topics.body: Univariate analysis describes one variable at a time (histogram, boxplot, counts). Bivariate analysis compares two (scatter, grouped summary). interview.q: Why does correlation not imply causation?
interview.answer: Two variables can move together because a third variable drives both, because of selection in the sample, or by coincidence. Establishing causation needs a design such as randomisation or a defensible causal model, not a large correlation coefficient.

interview.q: What is the difference between data missing at random and data missing not at random?

Missing not at random means the missing value itself drives whether it is missing, such as high earners refusing to report income; that needs a stronger assumption or a sensitivity analysis.

modules.title: Data Preprocessing and Feature Engineering
modules.goal: Make features model-ready without leaking future or test information into training.

topics.title: Standardise a numeric feature
topics.body: Standardisation subtracts the mean and divides by the standard deviation, giving a feature with mean 0 and standard deviation 1. Fit those statistics on training data only, then apply the same numbers at inference.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
x = np.array([1.0, 2.0, 3.0])
print([round(float(v), 2) for v in (x - x.mean()) / x.std()])

topics.title: One-hot encode a category
topics.body: One-hot encoding creates one binary column per category so a model does not invent an order between labels. Drop one column when a linear model has an intercept to avoid perfect collinearity, and handle unseen categories at inference.
topics.code:
import pandas as pd
df = pd.DataFrame({"color": ["red", "blue"]})
print(list(pd.get_dummies(df["color"]).columns))

topics.title: Data leakage and train/inference consistency
topics.body: Leakage is any information in training that will not be available at prediction time, or any statistic computed using test rows. Examples: scaling before splitting, target-derived features, future dates, and imputing with the full-dataset mean. Build one preprocessing object, fit it on training data, and reuse it unchanged for validation, test and production.

interview.q: Why must an imputer or scaler be fitted on training data only?
interview.answer: Fitting on all rows lets test-set statistics influence training, producing an optimistic estimate that will not reproduce in production. Fit on training data, then transform validation, test and live inputs with the same stored parameters.

interview.q: Why is one-hot encoding usually preferred over integer codes for unordered categories?
interview.answer: Integer codes imply an order and a distance: a model may treat “blue = 2” as twice “red = 1” and can interpolate a category that does not exist. One-hot encoding gives each category its own binary column, removing the false ordering at the cost of more columns.

print([(x - lo) / (hi - lo) for x in xs])
coding.hint: (x - min) / (max - min).

modules.title: ML Workflow and Model Fundamentals
modules.goal: Frame a problem, split honestly, establish a baseline, diagnose fit and run reproducible experiments.

topics.title: A chronological split for ordered data
topics.body: Rows are not always interchangeable. For time-ordered data, train on the past and test on the future; a random split can let the model learn from tomorrow to predict yesterday.
topics.code:
rows = list(range(10))
train, test = rows[:8], rows[8:]
print(len(train), len(test))

topics.title: A majority-class baseline
topics.body: Before any model, predict the most common class. This exposes imbalance and gives every later model a number it must beat on the same metric and split.
topics.code:
y = [1, 1, 0, 1]
print(round(max(y.count(0), y.count(1)) / len(y), 2))

topics.title: Overfitting, underfitting and cross-validation
topics.body: Underfitting misses the pattern in both training and validation. Overfitting captures noise, scoring high on training and lower on held-out data. K-fold cross-validation rotates the validation fold, giving a more stable estimate and a way to compare candidates without touching the test set.

interview.q: Why use stratified splitting for a classification problem?
interview.answer: Stratification preserves the class proportions in each split. With rare classes, a random split can leave almost none in validation or test, making the metric unstable or undefined. Stratify on the target when classes are imbalanced.

interview.q: What is data leakage, and what is one concrete example?
interview.answer: Data leakage is information from the target or the test period entering training, making validation look better than production. Scaling or imputing with statistics computed on the full dataset before the split is a common example; fit those steps on training data only.

modules.title: Linear Regression
modules.goal: Fit and interpret a linear model, calculate its errors and check the assumptions behind its coefficients.

topics.title: Fitting a line
topics.body: Simple linear regression chooses a slope and intercept that minimise squared error. `polyfit` with degree 1 is a compact way to see the fitted equation on a tiny dataset.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
x = np.array([1, 2, 3])
y = np.array([2, 4, 6])
m, b = np.polyfit(x, y, 1)
print(round(float(m), 1), round(float(b), 1))

topics.title: Mean squared error
topics.body: MSE averages the squared residuals. Squaring punishes large misses more than small ones, and the result is in squared target units; RMSE returns to the original unit.
topics.code:
y = [3, 5, 7]
p = [2, 5, 8]
print(round(sum((a - b) ** 2 for a, b in zip(y, p)) / len(y), 2))

topics.title: R-squared, residuals and assumptions
topics.body: R² is the fraction of target variance explained relative to a mean baseline, but it can look high on a poor model and does not prove causation. Linear regression assumes a roughly linear relationship, independent errors, constant variance and no severe multicollinearity. Plot residuals; a pattern means the model is missing structure.

interview.q: What does R-squared not tell you?
interview.answer: It does not tell you whether the model is causally correct, whether predictions are useful at the decision threshold, or whether the assumptions hold. It can be inflated by adding features and can be low even when the model captures the business signal. Inspect residuals and use an error metric in target units.

interview.q: What does the intercept represent in a linear regression?
interview.answer: It is the prediction when every feature is zero. It anchors the line so the slope does not have to pass through the origin; in data where zero is outside the observed range, it is a mathematical anchor rather than a business-meaningful prediction.

# print slope
coding.solution:

x = np.array([1, 2, 3])
y = np.array([3, 5, 7])
slope, intercept = np.polyfit(x, y, 1)
print(round(float(slope), 1))
coding.hint: Degree 1 returns slope first.

coding.title: Predict from a fitted line
coding.statement: For slope 2.5, intercept -1 and x = 4, print the prediction.

slope = 2.5
intercept = -1
x = 4
# print the prediction
coding.solution:
slope = 2.5
intercept = -1
x = 4
print(slope * x + intercept)
coding.hint: Multiply the input by the slope, then add the intercept.

defense.answer: R² measures explained variance on one sample, not the decision cost, calibration, fairness or stability in production. A model can explain variance overall while being systematically wrong for a subgroup or unusable when inputs drift.

topics.title: Ridge, Lasso and Elastic Net
topics.body: L2 (Ridge) shrinks coefficients smoothly and handles correlated features well. L1 (Lasso) can set coefficients exactly to zero, performing selection. Elastic Net mixes both. All three need scaling, and the penalty strength must be tuned with cross-validation.

interview.q: When would you prefer Lasso to Ridge?
interview.answer: Prefer Lasso when you suspect many features are irrelevant and want a sparse, interpretable model. Prefer Ridge when many features have small effects or are correlated, because L1 can arbitrarily keep one and drop another. Elastic Net is a compromise.

interview.q: Why does Lasso produce zero coefficients while Ridge usually does not?
interview.answer: Lasso adds an L1 penalty, whose diamond-shaped constraint reaches corners where some coefficients are exactly zero. Ridge’s L2 penalty has a circular constraint that shrinks coefficients smoothly, rarely all the way to zero. Lasso therefore performs selection; Ridge is better when many small effects should remain.

modules.title: Logistic Regression
modules.goal: Predict probabilities for binary outcomes, choose a threshold and interpret odds and log loss.

topics.title: The sigmoid function
topics.body: Logistic regression turns a linear score into a probability with the sigmoid. A score of zero maps to 0.5; large positive scores approach 1 and large negative scores approach 0.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
z = 0.0
print(round(float(1 / (1 + np.exp(-z))), 2))

topics.title: Applying a decision threshold
topics.body: A predicted probability becomes a class only after a threshold is chosen. The default 0.5 is not sacred; choose the threshold from the relative cost of false positives and false negatives.
topics.code:
p = 0.62
threshold = 0.5
print(int(p >= threshold))

topics.title: Log loss and odds
topics.body: Log loss punishes confident wrong probabilities heavily, which is why it is preferred to accuracy for probability models. Odds are p/(1-p); the model is linear in log-odds. Regularisation and scaling apply just as they do in linear regression.

interview.q: Why not use linear regression for a binary target?
interview.answer: A linear model can predict values below 0 or above 1, and its squared-error assumptions do not match binary outcomes. Logistic regression models a probability through the sigmoid and uses log loss, giving calibrated scores and a principled decision threshold.

interview.q: How do you interpret a logistic regression coefficient on the log-odds scale?
interview.answer: Holding the other features fixed, a one-unit increase in that feature changes the log-odds of the positive class by the coefficient. The odds multiply by exp(coefficient); a positive coefficient raises the probability, but the size of the probability change depends on the current score.

modules.title: Decision Trees and Ensemble Learning
modules.goal: Understand impurity, splitting, bagging and boosting, and choose a tree ensemble for tabular data.

topics.title: Gini impurity for a balanced split
topics.body: Gini impurity measures how mixed a node is. A node with a 50/50 class mix has impurity 0.5; a pure node has 0. Trees choose splits that reduce impurity.

topics.title: Entropy of a balanced node
topics.body: Entropy measures uncertainty in bits. A balanced binary node has entropy 1; a pure node has 0. Information gain is the impurity before a split minus the weighted impurity after it.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
p = 0.5
print(round(float(-p * np.log2(p) - (1 - p) * np.log2(1 - p)), 2))

topics.title: Bagging, random forests and boosting
topics.body: Bagging trains many models on bootstrap samples and averages them, reducing variance. A random forest adds feature subsampling to decorrelate trees. Boosting fits trees sequentially, each correcting the previous errors; it can be more accurate but needs careful learning rate, depth and early stopping. XGBoost, LightGBM and CatBoost are engineered boosting implementations.

interview.q: What is the main difference between a random forest and gradient boosting?
interview.answer: A random forest builds trees independently on bootstrapped samples and averages them, mainly reducing variance. Gradient boosting builds trees sequentially, each fitted to the current residual or gradient, mainly reducing bias. Boosting often wins on tabular accuracy but is more sensitive to tuning and overfitting.

interview.q: Why can a very deep decision tree overfit?
interview.answer: It can keep splitting until leaves are almost pure, fitting idiosyncratic noise and rare training rows. The tree then has high variance and poor generalisation. Limit depth, require a minimum number of samples per leaf, or prune and validate.

modules.title: Model Evaluation and Hyperparameter Optimization
modules.goal: Choose metrics that match real costs, read confusion matrices and tune without contaminating the test set.

topics.title: Precision and recall from counts
topics.body: A confusion matrix counts true positives, false positives, true negatives and false negatives. Precision is TP/(TP+FP); recall is TP/(TP+FN). They answer different operational questions.
topics.code:
tp, fp, fn = 40, 10, 10
print(round(tp / (tp + fp), 2), round(tp / (tp + fn), 2))

topics.title: F1 balances precision and recall
topics.body: F1 is the harmonic mean of precision and recall. It is useful when both matter, but it hides which error dominates; always show the confusion matrix and the business cost.
topics.code:
tp, fp, fn = 40, 10, 10
precision = tp / (tp + fp)
recall = tp / (tp + fn)
print(round(2 * precision * recall / (precision + recall), 2))

topics.title: ROC, AUC, PR curves and tuning
topics.body: ROC plots true-positive rate against false-positive rate across thresholds; AUC summarises ranking. On heavily imbalanced data, a precision-recall curve is often more informative. Tune with grid or randomised search inside cross-validation, and report the selected model once on the untouched test set.

interview.q: When is accuracy a poor metric?
interview.answer: When classes are imbalanced or error costs differ. A 99% accurate fraud model can miss every fraud. Use precision, recall, F1, PR-AUC or a cost-weighted metric that reflects what the product actually needs.

interview.q: Why is F1 not always the right metric?
interview.answer: F1 ignores true negatives, weights precision and recall equally, and treats every error as equally costly. In spam, fraud or medical screening the cost of a false positive and a false negative differs, so a cost-sensitive metric, PR-AUC or a threshold chosen for the decision may be more appropriate.

coding.title: Compute F1
coding.statement: For TP=40, FP=10 and FN=10, print F1 rounded to two decimals.
coding.solution:
tp, fp, fn = 40, 10, 10
precision = tp / (tp + fp)
recall = tp / (tp + fn)
print(round(2 * precision * recall / (precision + recall), 2))

coding.title: Specificity from a confusion matrix
coding.statement: For TN = 90 and FP = 10, print specificity.
coding.solution:
tn = 90
fp = 10
print(tn / (tn + fp))
coding.hint: Specificity is TN divided by all actual negatives.

precision = tp / (tp + fp)
print(round(2 * precision / (precision + 1), 2))
debug.error: This replaces recall with 1 and reports 0.89, not the F1 of 0.8. Compute both precision and recall from the same confusion counts.
debug.fix:
tp, fp, fn = 40, 10, 10
precision = tp / (tp + fp)
recall = tp / (tp + fn)

modules.title: Unsupervised Learning and Clustering
modules.goal: Find groups without labels, choose a sensible number of clusters and evaluate whether the groups mean anything.

topics.title: Assign points to the nearest centroid
topics.body: K-Means alternates between assigning each point to its nearest centroid and recomputing centroids as the mean of their members. The assignment step is a distance comparison.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
x = np.array([1, 4, 9])
c = np.array([0, 10])
print([int(np.argmin(abs(c - v))) for v in x])

topics.title: A simple silhouette-like separation
topics.body: A silhouette compares a point’s average distance to its own cluster with its distance to the nearest other cluster. Values near 1 mean tight, well-separated clusters; values near 0 mean overlapping clusters.
topics.code:
a, b = 2, 6
print(round((b - a) / max(a, b), 2))

topics.title: Elbow, hierarchical clustering and DBSCAN
topics.body: The elbow method plots within-cluster distance against K and looks for diminishing returns; silhouette gives a more direct quality score. Hierarchical clustering builds a merge tree you can cut at a chosen height. DBSCAN finds dense regions and labels sparse points as noise, without needing K, but struggles when densities vary.

interview.q: How do you choose K in K-Means?
interview.answer: Combine the elbow curve, silhouette score and domain usefulness. The elbow is suggestive, not decisive; silhouette can prefer a different K; and a segmentation with 12 neat clusters may be useless if the business can only act on four. Validate that the clusters differ on an outcome you care about.

interview.q: What assumptions does K-Means make about a cluster?
interview.answer: It assumes clusters are roughly spherical, have similar spread, and are well represented by their centroid; it also requires K in advance and is sensitive to feature scale and outliers. Violating these assumptions can produce confident but meaningless assignments.

modules.title: Dimensionality Reduction
modules.goal: Compress many correlated features into fewer components while keeping the variance that matters.

topics.title: Explained variance ratio
topics.body: PCA orders components by the variance they explain. A component with variance 4 beside one with variance 1 explains 80% of the total in this two-component example.
topics.code:
vals = [4, 1]
print(round(4 / sum(vals), 2))

topics.title: Centring before PCA
topics.body: PCA finds directions through the centre of the data. If features have different means, centring is mandatory; otherwise the first component can simply point at the mean offset.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
X = np.array([[1, 2], [3, 4]])
print((X - X.mean(axis=0)).sum(axis=0))

topics.title: Curse of dimensionality, t-SNE and UMAP
topics.body: As dimensions grow, distances become less discriminative and models need exponentially more data. PCA is linear and interpretable; t-SNE and UMAP are non-linear visualisation tools whose axes and distances should not be over-interpreted. Use PCA for compression and linear baselines; use t-SNE/UMAP for exploratory maps, not as proof of cluster truth.

interview.q: When would you use PCA instead of feature selection?
interview.answer: Use PCA when many features are correlated and you want a small number of components for compression, denoising or visualisation. Use feature selection when you must keep the original, interpretable columns, for example for a regulated explanation or a data-collection decision.

interview.q: What does a principal component represent geometrically?
interview.answer: It is a direction in the centred feature space that captures the largest remaining variance, with each later component orthogonal to the earlier ones. The first component is the best single linear direction for preserving variance, not necessarily the direction that best predicts a target.

coding.title: Variance share of the first component
coding.statement: Two components explain 3 and 1 units. Print the first component’s share rounded to two decimals.
coding.solution:
vals = [3, 1]
print(round(vals[0] / sum(vals), 2))
coding.hint: Divide by the total variance.

coding.title: Cumulative variance of two components
coding.statement: Explained variance ratios are [0.5, 0.3, 0.1]. Print the cumulative share of the first two components.
coding.solution:
ratios = [0.5, 0.3, 0.1]
print(sum(ratios[:2]))
coding.hint: Cumulative variance adds the ratios in component order.

debug.title: PCA on uncentred features

debug.error: This covariance-like matrix is computed around zero, not around the feature means. PCA needs centred data; otherwise the leading direction mixes the mean offset with real variation.

Xc = X - X.mean(axis=0)

learn.title: Curse of dimensionality, t-SNE and UMAP
learn.body: As dimensions grow, distances become less discriminative and models need exponentially more data. interview.q: When would you use PCA instead of feature selection?
interview.answer: Use PCA when many features are correlated and you want a small number of components for compression, denoising or visualisation. Use feature selection when you must keep the original, interpretable columns, for example for a regulated explanation or a data-collection decision.

interview.q: What does a principal component represent geometrically?
interview.answer: It is a direction in the centred feature space that captures the largest remaining variance, with each later component orthogonal to the earlier ones. The first component is the best single linear direction for preserving variance, not necessarily the direction that best predicts a target.

modules.title: Anomaly Detection
modules.goal: Find rare, unusual observations when labels are scarce, and evaluate the result without pretending it is supervised accuracy.

topics.title: A z-score flags a distance from the mean
topics.body: A z-score expresses how many standard deviations a point lies from the mean. It is simple and interpretable, but a single extreme point can inflate the mean and standard deviation, so robust alternatives matter.

topics.title: The IQR rule
topics.body: The interquartile range is robust to extreme values. Points below Q1 - 1.5×IQR or above Q3 + 1.5×IQR are commonly flagged for investigation, not automatically deleted.
topics.code:
import pandas as pd
s = pd.Series([10, 12, 11, 100])
q1, q3 = s.quantile([0.25, 0.75])
iqr = q3 - q1
print(int((s > q3 + 1.5 * iqr).sum()))

topics.title: Isolation Forest, LOF and evaluation without labels
topics.body: Isolation Forest isolates anomalies with random splits: unusual points need fewer splits. Local Outlier Factor compares local density, and One-Class SVM learns a boundary around normal data. Without reliable labels, evaluate with domain review, stability across seeds, alert volume and the cost of investigated false alarms; do not report supervised accuracy as if labels were complete.

interview.q: How do you evaluate anomaly detection when labels are unreliable?
interview.answer: Use a mixture of approaches: inspect a sample of alerts with domain experts, measure precision at a fixed review capacity, test stability across seeds and time, and track downstream outcomes. If a small labelled set exists, report precision/recall on it with its sampling bias made explicit; never treat missing labels as negatives.

interview.q: Why is accuracy a poor headline metric for anomaly detection?
interview.answer: Anomalies are rare, so predicting “normal” for every row can score very high accuracy while detecting nothing. Report precision, recall and PR-AUC on the anomaly class, plus the alert budget, because the cost of missed anomalies and false alarms is asymmetric.

debug.title: Dividing by zero standard deviation
debug.broken:
values = [5, 5, 5]
mean = sum(values) / len(values)
sd = (sum((v - mean) ** 2 for v in values) / len(values)) ** 0.5

modules.title: Feature Selection and Explainable ML
modules.goal: Keep features that carry real signal, explain model behaviour and avoid explanations that mislead.

topics.title: Correlation as a filter
topics.body: A correlation filter ranks numeric features by their linear association with the target. It is cheap and useful for screening, but it misses non-linear effects and can select redundant twins.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
x = np.array([1, 2, 3])
y = np.array([2, 4, 6])
print(round(float(np.corrcoef(x, y)[0, 1]), 2))

topics.title: Permutation importance as a drop
topics.body: Permutation importance measures how much a held-out metric falls when one feature’s values are shuffled. A large drop means the model relied on that feature; a near-zero drop means it could be noise or a duplicate.
topics.code:
base, permuted = 0.9, 0.7
print(round(base - permuted, 2))

topics.title: Filters, wrappers, embedded methods and SHAP
topics.body: Filter methods score features without a model; wrapper methods search feature subsets using model performance; embedded methods select during training (Lasso, tree importance). SHAP attributes a prediction to features using cooperative-game values, but correlated features can share credit unpredictably. Local explanations describe one prediction; global explanations summarise many, and neither proves causation.

interview.q: What is the difference between a local and a global explanation?
interview.answer: A local explanation answers why this one prediction happened, such as a SHAP waterfall for one applicant. A global explanation summarises the model across the dataset, such as mean absolute SHAP values or partial dependence. Local explanations can vary widely; global summaries can hide subgroup behaviour, so use both.

interview.q: Why can a feature with high correlation to the target still be useless in a multivariable model?
interview.answer: Its information may already be carried by another correlated feature, so its unique contribution is small. Correlation is also marginal and linear; a feature can look strong alone yet add nothing once interactions and other predictors are present. Check multivariable importance and redundancy, not just the pairwise correlation.

topics.title: Balanced class weight for a rare positive

topics.title: The positive base rate

topics.title: SMOTE, undersampling and cost-sensitive learning
topics.body: Random undersampling discards negatives and may lose information; oversampling duplicates positives and can overfit; SMOTE interpolates synthetic positives and must be applied only to training folds. Class weights avoid synthetic data. All approaches still require a threshold chosen for the operational cost, and precision-recall curves are more informative than accuracy.

interview.q: Why can accuracy be misleading on an imbalanced dataset?
interview.answer: Accuracy weights every row equally and is dominated by the majority class. A 99% negative dataset makes a constant-negative predictor 99% accurate while catching zero positives. Report positive-class precision/recall, PR-AUC or a cost-weighted metric instead.

interview.q: What is the difference between resampling and class weighting for an imbalanced target?
interview.answer: Resampling changes the training rows, either by duplicating the minority class or dropping majority rows; class weighting keeps the rows but makes minority errors count more in the loss. Both can improve minority recall, but both can distort predicted probabilities, so recalibration and validation are required.

modules.title: Time Series Machine Learning
modules.goal: Respect time order, build lag features and evaluate forecasts without leaking the future.

topics.title: Lag features
topics.body: A lag feature gives a model yesterday’s value when predicting today. It must be created with the correct time shift; using the current target as an input is leakage.
topics.code:

print(list(zip(x, x[1:])))

topics.title: A simple rolling mean
topics.body: A rolling statistic summarises the recent past. The mean of [1, 2, 3] is 2.0; on a real series, the window must end before the prediction timestamp.
topics.code:
x = [1, 2, 3]
print(sum(x) / len(x))

topics.title: Stationarity, ARIMA and time-based validation
topics.body: Stationarity means the series’ statistical behaviour is stable over time; differencing can remove trend. ARIMA combines autoregression, differencing and moving-average errors. Exponential smoothing weights recent observations more. Use time-based splits and rolling-origin cross-validation; random shuffling lets the model peek into the future.

interview.q: Why is a random train/test split dangerous for time series?
interview.answer: It mixes past and future rows, so the model can learn from future information and appear accurate while failing when deployed chronologically. Split by time: train on earlier periods, validate on later ones, and use rolling-origin validation for a realistic estimate.

interview.q: Why are lag features useful in time-series machine learning?
interview.answer: They give each row a controlled view of the past, such as yesterday’s demand or the value seven days ago, so a tabular model can learn temporal dependence. Lags must be built only from information available before the prediction time, or the model leaks the future.

coding.title: Create one lag

coding.title: Rolling mean of the last two values
coding.statement: For [10, 20, 30], print the rolling mean with a window of two, starting at the second value.
coding.solution:

print([(values[i - 1] + values[i]) / 2 for i in range(1, len(values))])
coding.hint: Each output averages the current value and the one before it.

defense.answer: Every feature at time t must be computable from information available before t. Use shifts, not centred windows; fit scalers on the training period; validate chronologically; and check that target-derived aggregates end before the prediction timestamp.

learn.body: Stationarity means the series’ statistical behaviour is stable over time; differencing can remove trend. ARIMA combines autoregression, differencing and moving-average errors. interview.q: Why is a random train/test split dangerous for time series?
interview.answer: It mixes past and future rows, so the model can learn from future information and appear accurate while failing when deployed chronologically. Split by time: train on earlier periods, validate on later ones, and use rolling-origin validation for a realistic estimate.

interview.q: Why are lag features useful in time-series machine learning?
interview.answer: They give each row a controlled view of the past, such as yesterday’s demand or the value seven days ago, so a tabular model can learn temporal dependence. Lags must be built only from information available before the prediction time, or the model leaks the future.

modules.goal: Recommend relevant items from behaviour and content, and evaluate ranking rather than just prediction.

topics.title: Cosine similarity
topics.body: Cosine similarity compares the direction of two vectors, ignoring magnitude. It is common for user-item behaviour because a user who interacts more should not automatically be “more similar” to everything.

import numpy as np
a = np.array([1, 0])
b = np.array([1, 1])
print(round(float(a @ b / (np.linalg.norm(a) * np.linalg.norm(b))), 2))

topics.title: Top-k ranking
topics.body: A recommender usually needs a short ranked list, not a score for every item. Sorting candidate scores and taking the first k is the final step after candidate generation.
topics.code:
scores = [0.9, 0.4, 0.8]
print(sorted(range(3), key=lambda i: scores[i], reverse=True)[:2])

topics.title: Content-based, collaborative and cold start
topics.body: Content-based filtering uses item attributes; collaborative filtering uses behaviour patterns across users or items. Matrix factorisation learns latent factors from the user-item matrix. A new user or item has no interactions, which is the cold-start problem; content features, popularity priors and exploration can help. Ranking metrics such as precision@k, recall@k and NDCG matter more than raw rating error.

interview.q: What is the cold-start problem?
interview.answer: A new user has no interaction history and a new item has no ratings, so collaborative signals are missing. Mitigate with content features, onboarding preferences, popularity fallbacks, exploration and careful logging; do not pretend a collaborative model has learned from zero interactions.

interview.q: What is the difference between content-based and collaborative filtering?
interview.answer: Content-based filtering recommends items similar to what a user liked using item features; collaborative filtering uses patterns across many users’ interactions, such as “users who liked this also liked that.” Collaborative filtering can find unexpected taste matches but struggles with new users or items; content features help with cold start.

modules.goal: Turn text into features, classify sentiment and evaluate a text pipeline without leaking the vocabulary.

topics.title: Token frequency with Counter
topics.body: A bag-of-words representation counts tokens and ignores order. Counter is a compact way to see the vocabulary and frequencies before vectorising.
topics.code:
from collections import Counter
print(dict(Counter("a b a".split())))

topics.title: A TF-IDF score
topics.body: TF-IDF raises the weight of a term that is frequent in a document but rare across documents. Here term frequency 0.2 times inverse document frequency 2 gives 0.4.
topics.code:
tf, idf = 0.2, 2
print(round(tf * idf, 2))

topics.title: Cleaning, stemming and evaluation
topics.body: Text cleaning removes markup, normalises case and handles punctuation. Tokenisation splits text; stopword removal drops very common words; stemming cuts suffixes aggressively while lemmatisation uses a dictionary and part of speech. Fit the vectoriser on training text only. Evaluate with precision, recall and F1 per class, and inspect misclassified examples for sarcasm, negation and domain language.

interview.q: What is the difference between stemming and lemmatisation?
interview.answer: Stemming applies crude suffix rules and may produce non-words (“studies” → “studi”). Lemmatisation maps a word to a valid dictionary form using linguistic information (“studies” → “study”). Lemmatisation is slower but more interpretable; stemming is a fast baseline.

interview.q: Why is TF-IDF often better than raw word counts for text classification?
interview.answer: TF-IDF downweights terms that appear in many documents, so common words such as “the” do not dominate, while terms frequent in one document but rare across the corpus receive more weight. It still produces a sparse, high-dimensional representation and does not understand word order or meaning.

interview.q: What is the difference between stemming and lemmatisation?
interview.answer: Stemming applies crude suffix rules and may produce non-words (“studies” → “studi”). Lemmatisation maps a word to a valid dictionary form using linguistic information (“studies” → “study”). Lemmatisation is slower but more interpretable; stemming is a fast baseline.

interview.q: Why is TF-IDF often better than raw word counts for text classification?
interview.answer: TF-IDF downweights terms that appear in many documents, so common words such as “the” do not dominate, while terms frequent in one document but rare across the corpus receive more weight. It still produces a sparse, high-dimensional representation and does not understand word order or meaning.

topics.title: A single perceptron step
topics.body: A perceptron computes a weighted sum and applies a step function. Here weights [1, -1] on inputs [1, 1] give 0, so the step output is 0. The bias would shift the threshold.

topics.title: A ReLU-like activation
topics.body: An activation introduces non-linearity. Without it, stacked linear layers collapse into one linear transformation. This compares each value with zero to produce [0, 0, 1].

topics.title: Backpropagation, embeddings and transformers
topics.body: Backpropagation applies the chain rule to compute each weight’s gradient, then an optimiser updates the weights. Embeddings learn dense vectors for categories or tokens. Transformers use attention to weigh context, which is why they power modern language models. Traditional ML remains the right first choice for many tabular problems; this module is a bridge to the separate BroCode Deep Learning course.

interview.q: Why is an activation function necessary in a neural network?
interview.answer: Without a non-linear activation, any stack of linear layers is equivalent to a single linear layer, no matter how deep. Activations let the network represent curved boundaries and complex interactions. ReLU, sigmoid and tanh are common choices with different gradient behaviour.

interview.q: What does backpropagation compute, and what does the optimiser do with it?
interview.answer: Backpropagation applies the chain rule to compute the gradient of the loss with respect to every weight. The optimiser uses those gradients to update the weights, for example with gradient descent or Adam; backpropagation computes direction, the optimiser decides the step.

modules.title: ML Pipelines, Engineering and Testing
modules.goal: Package preprocessing and models into reproducible, testable pipelines that behave the same in training and production.

topics.title: Function composition
topics.body: A pipeline is composition: the output of one step becomes the input of the next. This tiny example gives 7 because double(3) is 6 and add_one(6) is 7.

topics.title: Apply training statistics at inference
topics.body: A fitted transformation stores its training statistics. At inference, the same numbers are applied to a new value; recomputing the mean on live data would change the transformation and break train/serve consistency.
topics.code:
train_mean, live_value = 2.0, 4.0
print(round(live_value - train_mean, 2))

topics.title: Serialization, testing and train/serve skew
topics.body: A pipeline object should own imputation, encoding, scaling and the estimator so one `.fit` and one `.predict` reproduce the whole path. Joblib is common for scikit-learn artifacts; pickle can execute code, so never load untrusted files. Test schema, missing columns, unseen categories, numeric ranges and a known prediction. Train/serve skew is when production preprocessing differs from training preprocessing.

interview.q: What is train/serve skew and how do you prevent it?
interview.answer: It is any difference between the features a model saw in training and the features it receives in production: different units, fill values, category mappings or time windows. Prevent it by sharing one preprocessing pipeline, validating input schemas, logging the exact feature vector and comparing offline and online distributions.

interview.q: What is the difference between a transformer and an estimator in scikit-learn?
interview.answer: A transformer learns a feature transformation, typically with `fit` and `transform`, such as scaling or imputation. An estimator learns to predict a target with `fit` and `predict`. A Pipeline chains transformers into a final estimator so the same fitted preprocessing is used in training and inference.

checkpoint.q: Written checkpoint: explain train/serve skew and one pipeline practice that prevents it.
checkpoint.answer: Train/serve skew is when training and inference apply different preprocessing, feature order, defaults or model versions, so production inputs do not match what the model learned. Package preprocessing and the estimator in one pipeline, fit it once on training data, and reuse the same artifact and schema at inference. Log the feature contract and test a real request path.

logic.q: A scaler is fitted on all rows before the train/test split. Why is the resulting validation score optimistic?
logic.answer: The scaler has already seen the test rows’ mean and spread, so information from the evaluation set influenced training. That is preprocessing leakage; fit the scaler inside the training fold or pipeline, then transform the held-out data with those training statistics.

learn.title: Apply training statistics at inference
learn.body: A fitted transformation stores its training statistics. At inference, the same numbers are applied to a new value; recomputing the mean on live data would change the transformation and break train/serve consistency.

print(round(live_value - train_mean, 2))

learn.title: Serialization, testing and train/serve skew
learn.body: A pipeline object should own imputation, encoding, scaling and the estimator so one `.fit` and one `.predict` reproduce the whole path. Joblib is common for scikit-learn artifacts; pickle can execute code, so never load untrusted files. Test schema, missing columns, unseen categories, numeric ranges and a known prediction. Train/serve skew is when production preprocessing differs from training preprocessing.

interview.q: What is train/serve skew and how do you prevent it?
interview.answer: It is any difference between the features a model saw in training and the features it receives in production: different units, fill values, category mappings or time windows. Prevent it by sharing one preprocessing pipeline, validating input schemas, logging the exact feature vector and comparing offline and online distributions.

interview.q: What is the difference between a transformer and an estimator in scikit-learn?
interview.answer: A transformer learns a feature transformation, typically with `fit` and `transform`, such as scaling or imputation. An estimator learns to predict a target with `fit` and `predict`. A Pipeline chains transformers into a final estimator so the same fitted preprocessing is used in training and inference.

logic.q: A scaler is fitted on all rows before the train/test split. Why is the resulting validation score optimistic?
logic.answer: The scaler has already seen the test rows’ mean and spread, so information from the evaluation set influenced training. That is preprocessing leakage; fit the scaler inside the training fold or pipeline, then transform the held-out data with those training statistics.

topics.body: A health endpoint reports whether the service can serve traffic. It should be cheap and must not expose secrets or model internals. This dictionary is the shape a client can check.

print(status["status"])

topics.title: Docker, experiment tracking and drift
topics.body: Docker packages the API, dependencies and model artifact into a reproducible image; environment variables supply configuration without baking secrets into the image. MLflow tracks runs, parameters and artifacts and can host a model registry; DVC versions data and large artifacts alongside Git. In production, monitor input drift, prediction drift and delayed outcomes, then retrain only through a tested, versioned workflow.

interview.q: What is the difference between training and inference?
interview.answer: Training fits model parameters from historical data and is usually batch, compute-heavy and offline. Inference applies the frozen artifact to new requests, must be fast and reproducible, and must use exactly the training preprocessing. Training can be rerun; inference must be reliable and monitored.

interview.q: Why should a deployed model artifact be versioned together with its preprocessing?
interview.answer: A prediction depends on the exact estimator, feature order, encodings, imputation values and library versions used in training. Versioning only the model file makes rollback and reproduction ambiguous; version the whole pipeline and schema so a prediction can be traced to one reproducible artifact.

checkpoint.q: Written checkpoint: explain the difference between liveness and readiness, and why a model version should be recorded.
checkpoint.answer: Liveness says the process is running; readiness says it can actually serve traffic, including a loaded model and available dependencies. A 200 from a liveness endpoint does not prove the model artifact is present. Recording the model version and preprocessing version makes predictions reproducible, supports rollback and lets you investigate drift or incidents.
rubric: Distinguishes process health from ability to serve.

checkpoint.why: A live process can still be unable to predict; readiness and artifact provenance are separate operational guarantees.

logic.q: A health endpoint returns 200, but the model file it needs is missing. Is the service ready to serve predictions?
logic.answer: No. A liveness check can say the process is running, but readiness must verify the model artifact and dependencies. Return a failure from readiness and keep the service out of traffic until it can actually serve; a 200 that hides a missing model is a false health signal.

modules.title: Responsible AI, Capstone and Professional Readiness
modules.goal: Ship ML with privacy, fairness and explanation in mind, then prove your skills with a documented capstone.

topics.title: A demographic parity gap
topics.body: A fairness audit compares a metric across groups. Here one group’s positive rate is 0.6 and another’s is 0.4; the absolute gap is 0.2. This gap is a diagnostic, not a complete fairness verdict.
topics.code:
a, b = 60 / 100, 40 / 100
print(round(abs(a - b), 2))

topics.title: An accuracy gap across groups
topics.body: Overall accuracy can hide a group that the model serves badly. Reporting 0.9 for one group and 0.6 for another exposes a 0.3 gap that an aggregate score would obscure.
topics.code:
a, b = 0.9, 0.6
print(round(a - b, 2))

topics.title: Privacy, bias, security and the capstone
topics.body: Use only data you are permitted to use, minimise personal fields, and never expose sensitive records in notebooks or logs. Bias can enter through sampling, labels, proxies and deployment context; fairness metrics conflict, so document the chosen definition and its trade-offs. Model security includes input validation, artifact provenance and rate limits. A capstone is ready when the problem, data, split, baseline, metric, error analysis, limitations and a reproducible run are all documented.

interview.q: What are the limits of explainability?
interview.answer: An explanation describes the model’s behaviour, not the causal effect of a feature or the correctness of the data. Correlated features can share credit arbitrarily, local explanations can disagree with global ones, and a plausible explanation can still justify a harmful decision. Use explanations alongside audits, domain review and outcome monitoring.

interview.q: What is the difference between fairness through unawareness and measuring disparate impact?
interview.answer: Fairness through unawareness removes a protected attribute from the model, but proxies such as postcode, school or usage patterns can still encode it. Disparate-impact analysis measures outcomes across groups, exposing gaps that removing a column cannot prove are absent.

coding.title: Compute a parity gap
coding.statement: Positive rates are 0.7 and 0.5. Print the absolute gap rounded to two decimals.
coding.solution:
a, b = 0.7, 0.5
print(round(abs(a - b), 2))
coding.hint: Take the absolute difference.

coding.title: Disparate impact ratio
coding.statement: Positive rates are 0.6 and 0.3. Print the ratio of the lower rate to the higher rate, rounded to two decimals.
coding.solution:
rate_a = 0.6
rate_b = 0.3
print(round(min(rate_a, rate_b) / max(rate_a, rate_b), 2))
coding.hint: Divide the smaller rate by the larger one.

checkpoint.q: Written checkpoint: explain the difference between demographic parity and equal accuracy, and why fairness still needs context.
checkpoint.answer: Demographic parity compares selection or positive-decision rates across groups; equal accuracy compares overall correctness within each group. A model can have equal accuracy while approving one group at a much higher rate, or equal rates while making different kinds of errors. The appropriate fairness question depends on the decision, the harm and the affected population, so multiple group-level metrics and context are needed.
rubric: Defines demographic parity as comparable selection or positive rates.
Defines equal accuracy as comparable correctness, and notes that the two can diverge.
States that fairness depends on context, harms or the decision, not one universal metric.
checkpoint.why: Parity and accuracy measure different things; neither alone establishes fair treatment.

logic.q: A model has equal accuracy for groups A and B, but it approves group A at twice the rate. Does equal accuracy prove the model is fair?
logic.answer: No. Equal accuracy can coexist with very different selection rates, error types or false-positive costs. Fairness depends on the decision and the harm; report outcome rates, error rates by group and sample sizes before making a claim.

defense.answer: State the user and decision, the data and its limitations, the baseline, the chosen model and why, the metric and its business meaning, the error analysis, the subgroup/fairness checks, and how you would deploy and monitor it. checkpoint.q: True or false: equal accuracy across two groups proves that the model approves both groups at equal rates.
checkpoint.why: Accuracy and selection rate are different metrics. A model can be equally accurate while approving one group much more often, or vice versa.

checkpoint.q: Written checkpoint: explain the difference between demographic parity and equal accuracy, and why fairness still needs context.
checkpoint.answer: Demographic parity compares selection or positive-decision rates across groups; equal accuracy compares overall correctness within each group. A model can have equal accuracy while approving one group at a much higher rate, or equal rates while making different kinds of errors. The appropriate fairness question depends on the decision, the harm and the affected population, so multiple group-level metrics and context are needed.
checkpoint.why: Parity and accuracy measure different things; neither alone establishes fair treatment.
rubric: Defines demographic parity as comparable selection or positive rates.
Defines equal accuracy as comparable correctness, and notes that the two can diverge.
States that fairness depends on context, harms or the decision, not one universal metric.
